technique.how: Inspect for abdominal distension and palpate for a tense, non-compressible, drum-like abdomen; note rising peak airway pressures, oliguria, and falling cardiac output as supporting signs. Judge as 'elevated IAP' or 'normal'; then measure bladder (intravesical) pressure supine at end-expiration with 25 mL saline, transducer zeroed at the mid-axillary line.
technique.prerequisites: Foley catheter for confirmatory intravesical pressure; knowledge of risk factors (massive resuscitation, laparotomy, pancreatitis, ascites, obesity).
technique.contraindications: None for the exam; bladder pressure unreliable with neurogenic bladder, bladder trauma, or pelvic packing.

interpretation.positive_finding: A tense, distended abdomen judged clinically as 'raised pressure' is moderately specific (0.81-0.94) for IAH and, with new AKI or high airway pressures, should prompt immediate bladder-pressure measurement and consideration of abdominal compartment syndrome.
interpretation.negative_finding: A soft or non-distended abdomen does not exclude IAH: sensitivity is only 0.40-0.61, so at-risk ICU patients need measured bladder pressure regardless.
interpretation.pitfalls: Clinicians underestimate IAP; obesity, ascites, and post-laparotomy dressings confound palpation, and threshold definitions (IAP >10, >15, >=18 mmHg) differ between studies. WSACS defines IAH as sustained IAP >=12 mmHg and ACS as >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive exam in an at-risk patient: measure bladder pressure now and escalate for ACS; negative exam should not stop protocolized IAP monitoring in at-risk ICU patients.

estimates.population: 42 adult blunt-trauma ICU patients (mean ISS 36), 147 paired daily assessments; prospective blinded
estimates.quote: sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value and accuracy of clinical abdominal examination for identifying elevated IAP were 40%, 94%, 76%, 77% and 77%

estimates.target_condition: Significantly elevated intra-abdominal pressure (bladder pressure >15 mmHg)
estimates.population: 42 adult blunt-trauma ICU patients (mean ISS 36), 147 paired daily assessments; prospective blinded
estimates.quote: sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value and accuracy of 56%, 87%, 35%, 94% and 84% respectively, for significantly elevated IAP

estimates.population: 110 post-operative ICU patients at a trauma center, 150 clinical estimates of IAP; prospective blinded
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.609/(1-0.805) = 3.1; LR- = (1-0.609)/0.805 = 0.49; prevalence: IAP 'elevated in 21%' of 150 estimates
estimates.quote: which was elevated in 21%. The kappa score was 0.37; sensitivity, 60.9%; specificity, 80.5%; ppv, 45.2%; npv, 88.6%.

sources.citation: Kirkpatrick AW, Brenneman FD, McLean RF, Rapanos T, Boulanger BR. Is clinical examination an accurate indicator of raised intra-abdominal pressure in critically injured patients? Can J Surg. 2000.
Sugrue M, Bauman A, Jones F, Bishop G, Flabouris A, Parr M, et al. Clinical examination is an inaccurate predictor of intraabdominal pressure. World J Surg. 2002.

Kirkpatrick AW, Roberts DJ, De Waele J, Jaeschke R, Malbrain ML, De Keulenaer B, Duchesne J, Bjorck M, et al. Intra-abdominal hypertension and the abdominal compartment syndrome: updated consensus definitions and clinical practice guidelines from the World Society of the Abdominal Compartment Syndrome. Intensive Care Med. 2013.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a soft abdomen to exclude IAH/ACS in any ICU patient with risk factors (massive fluids, laparotomy, pancreatitis, burns, ascites) and new oliguria or rising airway pressures.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Tense abdomen with oliguria, rising ventilator pressures, or hemodynamic deterioration: urgent bladder pressure and surgical consultation for possible decompressive laparotomy.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Sugrue 2002: agreement between clinical estimate and measured IAP kappa 0.37 (Abstract, Results); between-examiner kappa not reported.

extraction_notes: Both primary studies are single-center ICU cohorts with repeated measurements per patient (unit of analysis is the assessment, not the patient), so CIs are not reported and prevalence is per measurement. Thresholds differ (>10, >15, >=18 mmHg) and predate the WSACS 2013 definition of IAH (>=12 mmHg); no pooled estimate exists to my knowledge. Full texts not open access via PMC, so all quotes/locations are from abstracts. WSACS 2013 (PMID 23673399) recommends IAP measurement rather than clinical estimation in at-risk patients; the 'IAH >=12 mmHg / ACS >20 mmHg' definitions are from that guideline (unverified recall of exact wording; not in abstract).
